# 300-unit-per-second roll-to-roll manufacturing of visible metalenses

https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10369-y

Received: 7 May 2025

Accepted: 5 March 2026

Published online: 15 April 2026

Check for updates

Trung Hoang $^{1,12}$ , Yujin Park $^{2,12}$ , Joohoon Kim $^{2,12}$ , Han Truong $^{1,3}$ , Sajjan Parajuli $^{1,4}$ , Beniel Jones Rajasekaran $^{4,5}$ , Kyungtae Kim $^{2}$ , Dohyun Kang $^{2}$ , Gyoseon Jeon $^{6}$ , Kyung-il Lee $^{6}$ , Dong Hyun Yoon $^{6}$ , Inki Kim $^{1,3,4,7}$ , Junsuk Rho $^{2,8,9,10,11}$ & Gyoujin Cho $^{1,3,4}$

Metasurfaces have been extensively studied over the past decade for their ability to manipulate light at subwavelength scales $^{1}$ . One of the most critical trends emerging recently has been scalable manufacturing, which is paving the way for the commercialization and industrial adoption of metasurfaces $^{2,3}$ . However, the production throughput of metasurfaces has so far largely remained at the academic level, limiting their practical deployment. Here we demonstrate the roll-to-roll nanoimprinting of visible metalenses for large-scale, cost-effective and fully automated manufacturing at industrial-level throughput. Our system achieves a production rate of 300 metalenses per second, with a cost comparable with—or even lower than—that of conventional refractive optics. A conformal high-index titanium dioxide layer is deposited via atomic layer deposition to dramatically enhance optical performance. Experimental characterization confirms high optical efficiency and uniformity across the full patterned area, with consistently high yields. This work shows potential for the transition of metasurface technology from academic research to the real world.

Metasurfaces, composed of two-dimensional arrays of subwavelength nanostructures, have redefined the way we manipulate light. Their ability to engineer phase, amplitude and polarization at the nanoscale has enabled compact and multifunctional alternatives to conventional optical components. Over the past two decades, their potential has been widely explored across a range of applications, including waveguide $^{4}$ , lensing $^{1,5}$ , holography $^{6,7}$ , beam deflection $^{8}$ , colour filtering $^{9,10}$ and imaging $^{11-15}$ . Among these, metalenses are compact, lightweight alternatives to bulky conventional lenses, enabling advanced functions such as high numerical aperture $^{16,17}$ , achromatic imaging $^{18-20}$ , tunable focus $^{21}$ and edge detection $^{22}$ . However, despite their remarkable performance, the transition of metasurfaces to industrial-scale applications remains hindered by fabrication complexity, low throughput and high manufacturing costs.

Early efforts in scalable fabrication explored bottom-up assembly and randomized nanoparticle approaches $^{23,24}$ , offering throughput benefits at the expense of structural precision and design flexibility. At the other end of the spectrum, deep-ultraviolet photolithography provides wafer-scale high-fidelity metasurface patterning, but its reliance on expensive semiconductor processes makes it economically infeasible for many optical applications $^{25-27}$ . Nanoimprint lithography (NIL) has emerged as a promising alternative to address this gap $^{28-33}$ . Using photolithographically fabricated metasurfaces as master moulds, NIL enables rapid and cost-effective replication $^{34,35}$ . Plate-to-plate NIL, for example, allows full 300 mm wafer-scale mould duplication in under 15 min, although it suffers from manual variability and limited automation $^{2,36}$ .

Semi-automated roll-to-plate NIL offers greater consistency by automating imprint and release steps while still requiring manual substrate loading $^{3}$ . Despite faster processing (about 1 min per wafer) and improved process control over plate-to-plate methods, its lens-level throughput (about 16 lenses per min) is constrained by the 4-inch wafer size. Looking further ahead, roll-to-roll (R2R) NIL has been explored for lower-resolution metasurface functions such as radiative cooling $^{37}$ , but not yet for complex phase modulation devices such as metal-enses. R2R NIL has emerged as an advanced manufacturing technique to overcome existing limitations by enabling low-cost, continuous and high-throughput replication of large-area nanoscale patterns on flexible substrates for industrial-scale applications $^{38,39}$ . It also provides more precise control over imprinting pressure, especially when operating at speeds that are 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than conventional plate-to-plate NIL $^{40}$ . However, the main bottleneck remains the fabrication of electroformed nickel mould for R2R systems, which becomes prohibitively expensive at large scales, potentially offsetting the cost advantage NIL was intended to provide.

Here, we demonstrate the industrial-scale mass production of centimetre-scale visible metalenses using R2R NIL. Our custom-built R2R NIL system operates at a web width of up to 300 mm and achieves a

This study contributes to significant progress in the scalable and sustainable manufacturing of metalenses, paving the way for the commercialization of metaphotonic devices.

chunks.heading: Manufacturing workflow
chunks.text:
## Manufacturing workflow

A schematic of the manufacturing workflow is shown in Fig. 1a. In step 1, a 300-mm wafer master stamp comprising 450 dies of 1-cm-diameter metalenses is fabricated using an ArF immersion scanner with a 4× reticle (Fig. 1ai, left). Next, a flexible replica mould is directly fabricated by UV-NIL using a master stamp (Fig. 1ai, right, and Extended Data Fig. 1). In step 2, the flexible replica mould is applied to our custom-built R2R-UV-NIL system, which is composed of three sections: resin coating, imprinting-curing unit and rewinding (Fig. 1aii and Supplementary Note 1). The 200-m-long metalenses produced on the PET film using the R2R system are shown in Fig. 1b,c, featuring vivid colours indicative of well-replicated nanostructures. Figure 1d,e displays the completed R2R-imprinted 300 mm wafer-scale metalens arrays and their scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images, respectively, confirming the successful fabrication of meta-atom structures.

chunks.heading: Design principle of metalens
chunks.text:
## Design principle of metalens

A 0–2π phase modulation of the metalens is achieved by rotating anisotropic meta-atoms by an angle of θ, which is known as the Pancharatnam–Berry phase. An anisotropic meta-atom rotated by an angle θ can be theoretically modeled using a Jones matrix. When right circularly polarized (RCP) light is incident, the complex transmittance can be expressed as follows (Supplementary Note 2).

$$
E _ {\mathrm{T}} = \frac {t _ {x x} + t _ {y y}}{2} \left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ - i \end{array} \right] + \frac {t _ {x x} - t _ {y y}}{2} e ^ {- i 2 \theta} \left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ i \end{array} \right]\tag{1}
$$

![](images/e39f11943532eafd192c658626de42f6052a5aae5d32fe8fa2dacf2e163ecd2b.jpg)

![](images/1c65c1375665288db9f6748d1f00b43d6b0364451d5a7b468a2c87404fdbe3fd.jpg)

![](images/29a61a1d1f09061db8385b6675521dddb50c6fbc06254819352848053da8ceee.jpg)

![](images/ddb0322dab4797fb58deb1c348ef107821b5911e34c908decc410f1254d0a43e.jpg)

where $t_{xx}$ and $t_{yy}$ represent the transmission coefficients for the incident light polarized along the x and y axes, respectively. The resulting electric field has two components: co- and cross-polarized light. The latter component, corresponding to left circularly polarized (LCP) light, undergoes a phase shift of $2\theta$ . Consequently, the full phase coverage can be achieved by rotating the anisotropic meta-atom from 0 to $\pi$ . As the phase modulation is governed solely by the cross-polarized component, the conversion efficiency ( $\eta$ ) is defined as the ratio of the transmitted cross-polarized light to the total incident light. Therefore, $\eta$ is calculated as follows:

$$
\eta = \left| \frac {t _ {x x} - t _ {y y}}{2} \right| ^ {2}\tag{2}
$$

Owing to the low refractive index (-1.5) of the imprint resins, meta-atoms composed solely of these materials (Fig. 2a) cannot effectively confine light within their structures (Fig. 2b). This weak light confinement results in an insufficient contrast between $t_{xx}$ and $t_{yy}$ , leading to a low achievable conversion efficiency (Fig. 2c). To address this limitation, we leverage the concept of a hybrid material $^{36}$ . When the imprinted meta-atoms are ALD-coated with TiO $_2$ , which has a high refractive index in the visible spectrum (Fig. 2d), light is strongly confined in the meta-atom (Fig. 2e). This enhanced confinement enables the phase difference between $t_{xx}$ and $t_{yy}$ to approach $\pi$ , resulting in significantly higher achievable conversion efficiency (Fig. 2f). Notably, even a thin 23 nm TiO $_2$ coating increases the efficiency dramatically from 10% to 90% in our designed meta-atom (period, 450 nm; height, 900 nm; length, 380 nm; width, 120 nm), and a target wavelength of 532 nm. This substantial improvement occurs because the difference in the effective refractive indices of the x- and y-polarized components increase with the thickness of the TiO $_2$ layer (Fig. 2g). Moreover, owing to the geometric nature of the $\theta$ phase, the designed meta-atoms feature broadband characteristics across the visible spectrum, demonstrating high efficiencies of 90% at 532 nm, and maintaining robust performance with 68% and 80% efficiencies at wavelengths of 450 and 635 nm, respectively (Fig. 2h).

PET film after the demoulding process (d) and collected metalens arrays at the rewinding unit (e). f–i, SEM images of a flexible polymer mould (f) and its cross section (h); R2R-imprinted metalens (g) and its cross section (i). Scale bars, 1 $\mu$ m. j, Colourful R2R-imprinted metalens on a PET roll at different viewing angles.

For the metalens to focus the cross-polarized light, the phase distribution $(\phi)$ of meta-atoms should follow the lens equation as:

$$
\phi_ {\text { ideal }} = - \frac {2 \pi}{\lambda} \left(\sqrt {x ^ {2} + y ^ {2} + f ^ {2}} - f\right),\tag{3}
$$

where $\lambda$ is the operating wavelength, $(x,y)$ are the coordinates of each meta-atom, and f is the focal length of the metalens. The meta-atoms at each position are rotated by $\theta=\frac{\phi_{ideal}}{2}$ to effectively focus the LCP light.

chunks.heading: Pilot line for R2R manufacturing of visible metalenses
chunks.text:
## Pilot line for R2R manufacturing of visible metalenses The complete R2R process of metalenses starts by dispensing and uniformly coating UV resin on the running PET film, followed by an imprinting process in which the film is pressed against the imprinting roller, with the pressure controlled by the counter roller and irradiated with UV light to cure the resin. A support roller facilitates the demoulding process to complete the pattern transfer from the replica mould to the PET web, which is finally collected at the rewinding roller (Fig. 3a–e). The performance of the UV-curable resin is one of the key factors affecting the accuracy and efficiency of the imprinting process. Therefore, an optimal UV resin for the R2R process is selected on the basis of key parameters such as viscosity, substrate adhesion and photocuring speed (Methods). Furthermore, a uniform coating of the resin on the substrate is critical for a successful imprinting process. A custom-made coating system is therefore used, consisting of a support roller and an interchangeable wire-wound metering rod (Mayer rod). This set-up precisely removes excess coating liquid and ensures that the replica mould is uniformly filled during the imprinting process (Fig. 3b). Refer to Supplementary Note 3 for details on the potential coating issues. Fabrication of replica moulds is one of the most important tasks in the manufacturing process, as it determines the main cost as well as the quality and resolution of the R2R system. chunks.heading: Pilot line for R2R manufacturing of visible metalenses
chunks.text: R2R-UV-NIL process $^{41,42}$ . However, this moulding technique is complex, time-consuming and extremely expensive, particularly for the high-resolution (40 nm) and large-area (300 mm wafer-scale) master stamps required for industrial applications. Furthermore, the sticking issues of the material considerably shorten the lifetime of nickel shim. Another candidate material for replica mould is h-PDMS; however, noticeable defects such as swelling and missing nanofeatures are observed during large-area replication (Supplementary Note 4). By contrast, replica moulds consisting of patterned polymer layers supported by a polymer substrate have attracted extensive industrial attention due to their much lower production costs. Here we fabricate a flexible polymer replica mould by directly replicating a master stamp using UV resin on a PET backplane foil. Our replica mould achieves a high quality of replication from the original master stamp, as confirmed by the SEM images (Fig. 3f,h and Extended Data Fig. 1). The replica mould is then treated with a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anti-stick coating to enhance release performance. To assess its durability during continuous imprinting, SEM images and atomic force microscopy (AFM) height profiles of the replica mould and imprinted structures have been taken before imprinting and after 200 m of use (Extended Data Figs. 2, 3 and Supplementary Note 5). Furthermore, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and contact-angle analyses (Supplementary Note 6) have been conducted to confirm the chemical and physical stability of the SAM coating throughout the process. The resulting SAM-coated replica mould is attached to the polyimide film as a tensioned belt and wrapped onto a metal imprinting roll with a width of 300 mm (Fig. 3c). A custom-designed UV system is then integrated to provide uniform illumination and support high-throughput processing (Supplementary Note 7 and Methods). In our system, the imprinting pressure is applied uniformly over a large area by precisely controlling the counter roller and sensor system. We optimize the imprint pressure at 45 kgf cm $^{-2}$ to minimize the residual layer thickness (329.67 ± 51.16 nm) and enable faithful replication of high aspect ratio features at a high speed (Supplementary Note 8). Under these carefully optimized conditions, the maximum web speed of the R2R system has been set at 200 mm s $^{-1}$ . As a proof of concept for scalable, high-throughput production, 300-mm-wide and 200-m-long metalens arrays have been successfully fabricated (Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Video 1) with faithfully reproduced meta-atoms (Fig. 3g,i). The vivid colours from strong light diffraction by the imprinted nanostructures are observed at different viewing angles (Fig. 3j), demonstrating the excellent quality of the replicated features.

chunks.heading: Characterization of the R2R-imprinted metalenses
chunks.text:
## Characterization of the R2R-imprinted metalenses

The focusing characteristics of the R2R-imprinted metalens are evaluated using a customized optical measurement set-up (Methods). Measured intensity profiles of the focal spots demonstrate that light is well-focused at the designed focal lengths, with clear focal points forming at 2.90 cm (450 nm), 2.45 cm (532 nm) and 2.05 cm (635 nm), corresponding to numerical apertures of 0.17, 0.20 and 0.24, respectively. The normalized intensity distributions of the focal plane demonstrate well-defined symmetric focal spots at all wavelengths (Fig. 4a). The symmetry and uniformity of these focal spots indicate high fabrication quality and alignment of the meta-atoms, which are crucial for achieving optimal focusing. The cross-sectional intensity profiles along the x-axis further confirm high-quality focusing, with the simulated results (dashed lines) showing excellent agreement with the measured data (solid lines) (Extended Data Fig. 4a). The close match between simulation and measurements validates our design approach and confirms the successful implementation of the geometric phase principle in the as-fabricated metalens. The full-width at half-maximum of the focal spots approaches the diffraction limit, indicating near-ideal focusing behaviour.

The imaging performance is quantitatively analysed by calculating the modulation transfer function (MTF) from the measured point spread function. The MTF, which characterizes the ability of the lens to transfer contrast at a particular resolution, is defined as the absolute value of the Fourier-transformed point-spread function normalized to its zero-frequency value. As shown in Extended Data Fig. 4b, the MTF of the fabricated metalens (solid lines) closely matches that of an ideal lens (dashed lines) for all three wavelengths, with good agreement at the design wavelength of 532 nm. Furthermore, the Strehl ratio is calculated to further evaluate the focal spot quality: the values of which are 0.9027, 0.8096 and 0.9179 for 450, 532 and 635 nm, respectively. These values, being above the Marechal criterion (Strehl ratio > 0.8), confirm that our R2R-imprinted metalens operates as a diffraction-limited imaging system across the visible spectrum. This indicates that our metalens can effectively resolve fine details across the visible spectrum, making it suitable for high-quality imaging. To experimentally validate the imaging performance of the R2R-imprinted metalens, we image a negative 1951 United States Air Fource (USAF) resolution target, covering all elements from groups 6 and 7, under 450, 532 and 635 nm illumination (Extended Data Fig. 5).

Given the large number of metalenses mass-produced via the R2R-UV-NIL process, it is essential to ensure consistent optical performance and uniformity. Qualitative inspection under white-light illumination of randomly selected 200-mm-wide sections confirms that all metalenses act as focusing elements (Fig. 4b). For quantitative evaluation, a $10 \times 10$ array in the central region of a 300 mm wafer-scale manufactured metalens array has an average focusing efficiency of 47.2% with a standard deviation of 3.2%, where only two out of 100 lenses have efficiencies below 40% (Fig. 4c). To assess large-area uniformity, focusing efficiencies measured along a single line across the entire 300 mm wafer-scale metalens array show an average of 49.4% with a deviation of 2.9%, confirming uniform performance across the wafer scale (Fig. 4d). Beyond a single wafer, reproducibility is examined by measuring four central lenses at different imprint lengths (50, 100, 150 and 200 m) along a 200-m roll, yielding consistent efficiencies of 51.5%, 47.5%, 48.3% and 47.0%, respectively (Extended Data Table 1). Finally, focusing efficiencies measured under various imprint pressures (5, 15, 30 and 45 kgf cm $^{-2}$ ) average 51.5%, 52.8%, 51.6% and 46.7%, respectively, confirming that imprint pressure has negligible influence on optical performance (Extended Data Table 2). Although differences between conversion and focusing efficiencies are expected, further discrepancies between simulated and measured results can arise from aliasing at the metalens level, phase-dependent meta-atom rotation causing weak coupling and fabrication-induced dimensional variations. These effects can be mitigated through optimized design and fabrication, enabling closer agreement between calculation and experiment.

chunks.heading: Discussion
chunks.text:
## Discussion

In summary, we demonstrate metalens fabrication at an industrial scale using a custom-built R2R nanoimprinter in a cost-effective, fully automated and high-throughput manner, with a throughput as high as 300 lenses per second (Supplementary Table 1). By carefully optimizing the mould preparation and key process parameters—including web speed, tension and imprinting conditions—we have successfully implemented an R2R system for metalens production, achieving feature resolution down to 80 nm. By applying a hybrid material composed of UV-curable resin and a conformal TiO $_{2}$ thin film, the optical performance of the metalenses has been significantly improved, achieving about 49% efficiency across a full 300-mm wafer.

Despite these advances, in situ metrology and quality control remain crucial for the mass production of metalenses, and further investigation into real-time monitoring of structural uniformity and optical efficiency are required $^{43}$ . Moreover, improving productivity in the deposition step remains another major challenge. In this work, a time-divided ALD process has been used to deposit the $TiO_{2}$ film; however, using a spatial-divided ALD system could further enhance the overall throughput of the R2R system $^{44-46}$ . The R2R manufacturing throughput can be systematically scaled by using larger imprint roller geometries in combination with optimized mould designs. Nevertheless, we believe this work marks an important milestone in advancing metasurface technology from research-scale to commercial applications, with significant implications for scalable meta-optical manufacturing.

chunks.heading: Methods
chunks.text: ## Methods

chunks.heading: Numerical analysis
chunks.text:
## Numerical analysis

The computational results presented here were obtained through numerical simulations using COMSOL Multiphysics v.6.0, which implements the finite-element method. Three-dimensional calculations were conducted in Cartesian coordinates with periodic boundary conditions applied to all sides.

chunks.heading: Master template preparation
chunks.text:
## Master template preparation

The initial template comprised molybdenum silicide deposited on a silica substrate. Metalens patterns were created using a high-resolution electron-beam lithography system (JBX Series, JEOL) to expose the positive photoresist (FEP series, Fujifilm). Following exposure, patterns were developed using a tetramethylammonium solution. Molybdenum silicide was then deposited to a thickness of 69 nm via electron beam evaporation, using a silicon substrate as the cluster formation template. Pattern transfer was accomplished using ArF immersion lithography (XT-1900Gi, ASML) on positive photoresists, followed by development in a tetramethylammonium solution.

chunks.heading: UV resin selection
chunks.text:
## UV resin selection

Among several commercial UV resins tested, mr-UVCur26SF (Micro Resist) was selected for its low viscosity, fast photocuring response (supporting web speeds up to 30 m min $^{-1}$ ), and high pattern fidelity under the R2R NIL conditions. The resin also showed strong adhesion to the PET substrate, enabling easy demoulding and eliminating the need for substrate pretreatment.

chunks.heading: R2R nanoimprint lithography
chunks.text:
## R2R nanoimprint lithography

Polyethylene terephthalate roll (V7610, 250 $\mu$ m thick) was purchased from lonefilm, Korea. The UV resin mr-UVCur26SF was purchased from micro resist technology. The flexible polymer shim was treated with trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich) to form a vapour-phase self-assembled monolayer for improved mould release. Two 300 mm wafer-scale replica moulds were attached to a long polyimide film (300 mm × 900 mm) using double-sided tape and wrapped around an embossing roller with a width of 300 mm. A rubber roller was used as a counter roller to ensure conformal contact during the process. When the resist-coated web was fed into the embossing roller, the web tension was precisely controlled while maintaining the imprint pressure at 45 kgf cm $^{-2}$ . This optimized pressure was also sufficient to prevent damage to the mould patterns. The resist was then cured by UV illumination positioned 5–7 mm from the embossing roller. A custom-built high-power UV system was used, consisting of a 365 nm UV light-emitting diode array with an intensity of 1,000 mW cm $^{-2}$ and >90% uniformity over a 300 × 94 mm area. The web speed was maintained at 200 mm s $^{-1}$ , and the cured resist and web were continuously separated from the mould at the support roller as the web moved forward.

chunks.heading: TiO $_{2}$ deposition
chunks.text:
## TiO $_{2}$ deposition

The nanostructured resin surface was coated with $TiO_{2}$ using a sequential thermal and plasma-enhanced ALD system (NexusBe; Nexus Plaminar Series). We used $\mathrm{Ti(NMe_{2})_{4}}$ as the titanium source material, and activated oxygen plasma (350 W, 1 Torr) was used as the oxidant.

The deposition sequence consisted of four steps: $\mathrm{Ti(NMe_{2})_{4}}$ precursor injection for 0.5 s, followed by argon purging for 15 s, then 5 s exposure to oxygen plasma and finally another 15 s argon purge. This process was performed at 80 °C, achieving a deposition rate of 1.0 Å per cycle.

chunks.heading: Optical measurement set-up
chunks.text:
## Optical measurement set-up

A spatial filtering set-up (Thorlabs, AC127-019-A; Thorlabs, P10CB) was used to generate a clean Gaussian beam from the incident laser. The collimated beam was then passed through a linear polarizer (Thorlabs, LPVISE050-A) followed by a quarter-wave plate (Thorlabs, AQWP05M-600) to produce LCP light. The LCP beam was normally incident on the metalens, and the transmitted light was collected by a commercial objective lens (Olympus, 1-U2M350). An analyser was inserted between the objective and the tube lens to isolate the conjugate RCP component corresponding to the point spread function (Thorlabs, TTL180-A). The resulting beam was imaged using a charge-coupled device camera (Lumenera, INFINITY2-1RC), and the intensity profiles at the focal plane were recorded for subsequent analysis.
